record.paper_title: Problems in Data Structures and Algorithms
record.original_question: Even if the full dynamic optimality conjecture remains open, can one prove that splaying achieves a log log competitive bound against the optimal offline binary-search-tree algorithm, analogous to the log log performance factor obtained by Demaine and collaborators for a different online search-tree update algorithm?

evidence.quote: They have designed an on-line search tree update algorithm that comes within a loglog performance factor of the optimal off-line algorithm (as compared to the log factor of a balanced tree algorithm).
An immediate question is whether one can prove a similar loglog bound for splaying, even if the dynamic optimality conjecture remains out of reach.

artifact.category_tag: competitive analysis of binary search trees
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the standard model of online binary search trees (BSTs) on a sequence of access requests over n keys, where the cost of an algorithm on a request sequence is the total number of nodes touched (including rotations performed) while servicing the requests. The offline optimum OPT(σ) is the minimum cost over all BST algorithms that know σ in advance. An online BST algorithm A is f(n)-competitive if there exist constants c,d such that, for every request sequence σ, the cost of A on σ is at most c·f(n)·OPT(σ) + d·|σ|.

The splay tree algorithm of Sleator and Tarjan is the online BST that, upon each access to a key x, performs the splay operation (the standard sequence of zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations) to move x to the root. The dynamic optimality conjecture asserts that splay trees are O(1)-competitive.

Question: prove or disprove that the splay tree algorithm is O(log log n)-competitive; that is, show that there exist absolute constants c,d such that for every n and every access sequence σ on n keys, the cost incurred by splaying on σ is at most c·(log log n)·OPT(σ) + d·|σ|.
artifact.status_search_result: The broader goal of obtaining an O(log log n)-competitive online BST has been achieved by algorithms other than splay trees themselves: Tango trees (Demaine, Harmon, Iacono, Pătraşcu) and Multi-Splay Trees (Wang, Derryberry, Sleator) are both proven O(log log n)-competitive, and chain-splay trees (Georgakopoulos) achieve O(log log n)-competitiveness for a splay-style algorithm against offline BSTs using rotations. However, the specific question of whether the original splay tree algorithm itself is O(log log n)-competitive remains open; only weaker bounds (such as those implied by the access lemma and known properties like the working-set, static-finger, and dynamic-finger theorems) are known for splaying.

status_evidence.title: O(log log n)-Competitive Dynamic Binary Search Trees
status_evidence.snippet: Multi-splay trees are O(log log n)-competitive, and amortized O(log n).
status_evidence.claim: An O(log log n)-competitive BST (multi-splay) exists, but the result is for a new variant, not for plain splay trees.

status_evidence.title: Chain-splay trees, or, how to achieve and prove log log N-competitiveness by splaying
status_evidence.snippet: Chain-splay is log log N-competitive to any off-line algorithm that maintains a binary search tree with rotations.
status_evidence.claim: A splaying-style algorithm (chain-splay) achieves O(log log N)-competitiveness, but this is a modification of plain splaying.

status_evidence.title: Splay tree - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The dynamic optimality conjecture ... Despite 20 years of research this conjecture is still unresolved.
status_evidence.claim: The competitiveness of plain splay trees beyond known specific bounds (and short of O(1)) remains unresolved; no O(log log n) bound is known for splaying itself.
